title: Sidh Gosht close
hookLine: a conversation with other seekers, still worth having

cards: Most conversations vanish. Somebody says goodnight, the porch light goes off, and whatever was said lives on only in the two people who were there. A few get written down.
Fewer still get sung. The talk between Guru Nanak and the Siddhs on the mountain did not vanish.
It sits in the Guru Granth Sahib, in Raga Ramkali, and Sikhs still read it and sing it: a conversation between seekers who did not agree, kept as scripture. For two weeks we've sat in that circle.
Today we stand and look back at it.

teach.h: WHO ARE YOU? THE DUCK STAYS DRY.
teach.b: Walk around the circle once. It began with a question as old as strangers: who are you, where do you come from. Asked how to live, Nanak gave the lotus and the duck: in the water, not soaked by it.
Asked why he left home, he said: to seek the Gurmukhs, the people turned toward the Guru. The yogis' earrings became the Guru's Word. Asked where it all began, he spoke of wonder.
Asked where the mind lives, he said the Word steadies it.
Then the answer some readers call the center of the whole dialogue: the Word is the Guru, and attention tuned to it is the disciple. The world as an ocean, the Word as the boat. A guide is needed.
The breath carries the Name. The true yogi is spotless in the middle of the soot. And, read beside a verse from the Asa di Var, the side that bows is the heavier one.
Notice what held all that together. Not agreement. The yogis never stopped being yogis, as far as the text tells us.
What held it was that both sides kept talking: real questions, real answers, in the other side's own language.

teach.h: CONVERSATION AS PART OF THE PATH.
teach.b: That may be the quietest teaching of the Sidh Gosht: a conversation with other seekers is worth having all the way through.
Sikhs keep it in scripture, beside the Gurus' hymns of praise. Talking honestly with people on a different path can be part of the path itself.

how: The Sidh Gosht is in Raga Ramkali in the Guru Granth Sahib; Sikhs read it in the course of a full reading of the scripture, and kirtan singers sing stanzas from it.

o: the yogis gave up their path and became Sikhs
Nanak won the debate and the yogis went quiet
a long dialogue held together by both sides talking

games.q: what's inside the Sidh Gosht — tap the pairs.

games.q: you and a friend walk different paths and disagree about a lot. what does the Sidh Gosht model?
o: avoid the subject to keep the peace.
argue until one of you gives in.
keep talking: real questions, real answers.
games.why: the yogis and Nanak never merge their paths in the text. what holds is the conversation itself, kept as scripture.

practice: Think of someone you'd like to really talk with, a friend who sees things differently, a parent, a neighbor whose faith isn't yours, and choose one real question the yogis might have asked: where do you come from, what steadies you, what's it all for.
Then imagine listening to the whole answer without planning your reply. If you pray, ask for an open ear; if not, simply hold the person in mind.

wordCard.voice: Sidh Gosht close. The end of the dialogue with the yogis: two paths that didn't agree, a conversation that held, and scripture that kept it. Today's word.

orig.note: the discourse with the Siddhs, the title as it stands in Raga Ramkali.

carryVoice: Your line: keep talking. A real question deserves the whole answer. Two weeks on the mountain, done.
